verdicts.notes:
I checked all 12 r1 cards (b1, sr1-01 to sr1-12) against the live pages on 2026-10-04. Status of the standards:
- WCAG 2.2 is the W3C Recommendation of 12 December 2024.
- WCAG 3.0 is a W3C Working Draft dated 10 September 2026. The draft itself says "WCAG 3 does not replace WCAG 2".
- The Understanding Conformance page was updated 20 September 2026.

Every URL loaded with status 200 and every answer is correct. Evidence for the cards that pass:
- sr1-03 (True), Recommendation 5.2.1: "For Level AA conformance, the web page satisfies all the Level A and Level AA success criteria, or a Level AA conforming alternate version is provided".
- sr1-04 (False), 5.2.2: "cannot be achieved if part of a web page is excluded".
- sr1-05 (True), 5.2.3: "all web pages in the process conform at the specified level or better". Its example is a checkout.
- sr1-06 (True), Understanding Conformance: alternate versions let authors provide "an accessible alternative page in technologies that are accessibility supported" and "may be provided to accommodate different technology environments".
- sr1-07 (False), 5.2.1 Note 2: "It is not recommended that Level AAA conformance be required as a general policy for entire sites".
- sr1-08 (False), Understanding Techniques: "Techniques are informative — that means they are not required", and content "does not have to use W3C's published techniques in order to conform".
- sr1-09 (False), Numbering in WCAG 2.2: "The order of success criteria within each guideline does not imply information about conformance level". The statement names the version.
- sr1-11 (False): the TR page header reads "W3C Working Draft 10 September 2026". Volatility is correctly may_change.

Four cards are flagged: sr1-01, sr1-10 and sr1-12 as weak (near-copies or giveaways) and sr1-02 for its source. All three weak-card replacements are True, so the section stays at 6 true and 6 false. No r1 fact repeats in r2 to r12; sr2-11 tests the level of Target Size (Enhanced), which is a different fact from sr1-03.

Minor points, not flagged:
- sr1-05 says "WCAG assesses", which makes WCAG the actor. That is acceptable but awkward.
- sr1-03 is easy, but its misconception (that Level AA means only the AA criteria) is realistic.

verdicts.notes:
I checked all 12 r2 cards (all in web-accessibility-b1.json). All 10 source URLs load (HTTP 200) and are official WAI Understanding pages for WCAG 2.2. I also checked each claim against the WCAG 2.2 Recommendation (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/, W3C Recommendation 12 December 2024). Its New Features list matches the levels the cards use: 2.4.11 AA, 2.4.12 AAA, 2.4.13 AAA, 2.5.7 AA, 2.5.8 AA, 3.2.6 A, 3.3.7 A, 3.3.8 AA, 3.3.9 AAA.

Cards that passed:
- 01: \"This AA criterion allows for the component receiving focus to be partially obscured\".
- 02: 2.4.12 is Level AAA.
- 03: \"a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 between the same pixels in the focused and unfocused states\". The explanation's contrast with adjacent colours (1.4.11) matches the Understanding page.
- 04: \"achieving keyboard equivalence for a dragging operation does not automatically meet this success criterion, unless that equivalent keyboard operation also provides controls that can be clicked or tapped\".
- 06: Inline exception, \"The target is in a sentence or its size is otherwise constrained by the line-height of non-target text\".
- 07: \"they occur in the same order relative to other page content, unless a change is initiated by the user\".
- 09: Note 2 of 3.3.8, \"Examples of mechanisms that satisfy this criterion include: support for password entry by password managers\".
- 10: 3.3.9 keeps only Alternative and Mechanism, and the Understanding page says object recognition and personal content \"are not excepted\".
- 11: 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced) is Level AAA, 44 by 44.

True/false balance is 6/6 and the suggested replacements keep it. Pure level cards in r2 are 02 and 11, within the cap of 4. Cards 02 and 11 share one false template (\"an (Enhanced) criterion is Level AA\"). That is the deck-wide maximum of two, and the prompt explicitly endorses both confusions, so I did not flag them. Note that the word \"Enhanced\" consistently marks AAA, which makes both cards easier than intended.

No r2 card shares a fact with any card in r1 or r3 to r12. No other deck card tests Parsing, target size, focus obscuring, authentication, help or redundant entry. 2.4.7 Focus Visible stays in r7 (sr7-05).

Minor point, not flagged: the sr2-07 explanation's phrase \"in the same page variation\" comes from Note 2, which concerns visual position. It is fine but could simply say \"across a set of web pages\".

The misconception is a strawman, not a confusion a learner who studied could hold. Explanation: "HTML permits only one main element without the hidden attribute per document, so a label cannot make a second visible main valid." factKey single-visible-main-element. verdicts.notes: I checked all 12 r3 cards (01 to 12): 6 true (01, 03, 06, 08, 10, 12) and 6 false (02, 04, 05, 07, 09, 11). All 4 suggested replacements keep the original answer, so the balance stays at 6 and 6. Every source URL loads, is official and current, and supports its card. ARIA in HTML (W3C Recommendation, 11 August 2026) confirms: a without href is generic; section is region only with an accessible name, otherwise generic; header is banner only when not a descendant of article, aside, main, nav or section, otherwise generic; h1 to h6 get aria-level from the number in the tag name; search maps to the search role. HTML-AAM (Working Draft, 23 September 2026) gives the heading level as \"the number in the element's tag name\", with no section-depth rule, so the false answer of 07 holds. The MDN Accessibility tree glossary supports 01 (\"Browsers then create an accessibility tree based on the DOM tree\"). The MDN region_role page supports 03. The MDN banner_role page supports 04 and says a nested header exposes generic. The MDN search page supports 05 (a container for search or filtering controls). Understanding 1.3.2 supports 08 (\"There may be more than one order that is 'correct'\"). MDN caption supports 10: caption gives the table \"an accessible name or accessible description\"; the card says \"title\", which is acceptable, but 10 is close to a giveaway, so a stronger version could test the accessible name directly. Cards 02, 04 and 07 are good distinction cards. No duplicates with other sections: r7-09 covers skip links and Bypass Blocks; r4-11 covers heading wording, not heading level. Coverage gaps in r3 that are not defects: no card covers lists, native button versus scripted div, 1.3.1 Info and Relationships by name, or the output-as-status mapping. The suggested replacement for 09 (single visible main) adds landmark coverage of main. The 4 flags are all weak_card (3 strawman or giveaway cards plus 1 near-truism). No wrong answers or source failures were found.

flagged.urlStatus: MDN aria-label page loads (200) and is current, but it does not state the card's fact
flagged.evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Reference/Attributes/aria-label says only "By default, a button's accessible name is the content between the opening and closing <button> tags ... If none of these options are available or if the default accessible name is not appropriate, use the aria-label attribute" and gives precedence only over iframe title, img alt and input label. It never says aria-label replaces rather than appends to a button's content. The APG does say it: https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/practices/names-and-descriptions/ : "If aria-label is applied to an element with one of the roles that supports naming from child content, content contained in the element and its descendants is hidden from assistive technology users."
flagged.problem: The answer (False) and the explanation are correct, but the cited page only implies the replace-versus-append fact and never states it. The card's whole point, that aria-label replaces the content-derived name, cannot be checked on the MDN page.
flagged.suggestedFix: Keep the statement and the answer (False). Change the source to https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/practices/names-and-descriptions/ (APG, Naming with a String Attribute Via aria-label). Optional explanation (176 chars): "If aria-label is set on a button, its value replaces the name the button would get from its content; the content is hidden from assistive technology users rather than appended."

flagged.urlStatus: APG names-and-descriptions page loads and is current, and supports the card
flagged.evidence: https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/practices/names-and-descriptions/ : "Elements having one of the following roles are, by default, named by a string calculated from their descendant content: button, cell, checkbox ..."
flagged.problem: The card is correct but gives itself away. Anyone who sees `<button>Save</button>` will answer True without knowing anything about accessible names, so for a working frontend developer it teaches nothing. Together with sr4-07, sr4-08 and sr4-09, it means most True cards in r4 are the obvious-sounding ones, which becomes a tell.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace with a True card on a non-obvious part of naming from content. Statement (108 chars): "Browsers include text that CSS inserts with `::before` in a `<button>` when computing its name from content." Explanation (190 chars): "When a name comes from content, the Accessible Name and Description Computation adds CSS-generated text from ::before and ::after, so icons or words inserted that way can end up in the name." Source: https://www.w3.org/TR/accname-1.2/ (step "Name From Generated Content": "For ::before pseudo elements, User agents MUST prepend CSS textual content"). Answer True, so the section stays at 6 True and 6 False.

flagged.urlStatus: MDN aria-describedby page loads and is current, and supports the card
flagged.evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Reference/Attributes/aria-describedby : "It is used to establish a relationship between widgets or groups and the text that describes them."
flagged.problem: This is a definition card: the attribute name 'describedby' tells you the answer, so a player who knows nothing about ARIA answers True. It tests no distinction, such as description versus name or hidden versus visible referenced text.

Explanation (183 chars): "Elements referenced by aria-describedby need not be visible: the description computation includes hidden referenced text, so a hint can reach assistive technology without being shown." verdicts.notes:
I checked all 12 r4 cards (6 True, 6 False). All source URLs load and are current official pages. Status found today: HTML-AAM is a Working Draft (23 September 2026), Accname 1.2 is a Working Draft (2 October 2026) and WAI-ARIA 1.2 is a Recommendation. The cards that pass:
- 02 (aria-labelledby beats aria-label): MDN says \"If an element has both attributes set, aria-labelledby will be used.\"
- 03 (label for matches id, not name): MDN says \"The value is the id of the labelable form control.\"
- 04 (placeholder fallback): HTML-AAM 4.1.1 reads \"If the accessible name is still empty: use the value of the control's title attribute. If the accessible name is still empty: use the value of the control's placeholder attribute.\" Its may_change setting is appropriate.
- 06 (generic prohibits naming): WAI-ARIA 1.2 lists generic with \"Prohibited States and Properties: aria-label, aria-labelledby, aria-roledescription\" and \"Name From: prohibited\".
- 08 (APG Rule 2): the page says \"Prefer Visible Text\" and that visible text \"simplifies maintenance, prevents bugs\".
- 09 (translation): the APG says \"When a user interface is translated into multiple languages, ensure that aria-label values are translated.\" It is easy and its True answer is guessable, but it is explicitly in scope, so it is kept.
- 10 (2.4.4, Level A): the SC text is \"from the link text alone or from the link text together with its programmatically determined link context\".
- 11 (2.4.6, Level AA): Understanding says it \"does not require that content acting as a heading or label be correctly marked up ... covered separately by 1.3.1\".
- 12 (2.5.3, Level A): Understanding says \"A best practice is to have the text of the label at the start of the name\". It lists interspersed words as a possible failure, but \"around\" (before or after) stays true.

I found no duplicates with other sections. sr3-03, sr9-02, sr9-08 and sr10-03 touch nearby topics but test different facts. The two replacements are distinct facts: CSS-generated content in names, and hidden text referenced by describedby. They do not mirror each other or any existing card. The scratch files in a scratch folder are only page downloads.

flagged.evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA: "The aria-valuenow describes the current state of it and therefore must be kept updated with JavaScript." https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Reference/Roles/checkbox_role: "The developer is required to change the value of the aria-checked attribute dynamically when the checkbox is activated."

It does not test the real misconception, which is that the browser updates ARIA states by itself. The source supports it only indirectly, through the aria-valuenow progressbar example.

Explanation: "MDN says the developer must change aria-checked dynamically when a custom checkbox is activated. The role describes the state, but browsers do not maintain it for the author." Source: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Reference/Roles/checkbox_role

The realistic misconception is that hiding a redundant focusable control, such as a duplicate link, from assistive technology is fine.

Explanation: "MDN warns against aria-hidden="true" on focusable elements and their ancestors: keyboard users would land on a control that assistive technology does not expose." Same URL.

The example is marked NOT RECOMMENDED: "<!-- Avoid doing this! --><button role="button">...</button>". The nav row reads: "(navigation is also allowed, but NOT RECOMMENDED.)"

It claims the spec actively recommends <button role="button"> "for clearer accessibility semantics", which few studied developers would accept. The realistic misconception is the old habit of adding redundant landmark roles (nav role=navigation) for older assistive technology. appliesTo says "WAI-ARIA 1.2", but the fact comes from ARIA in HTML.

Explanation: "ARIA in HTML marks a role that repeats an element's implicit role, such as navigation on nav, as NOT RECOMMENDED. The nav element already exposes the navigation landmark." Source: https://www.w3.org/TR/html-aria/#el-nav

verdicts.notes: I checked all 12 r5 cards, all in web-accessibility-b2.json. The section is balanced at 6 true (01, 04, 07, 08, 11, 12) and 6 false (02, 03, 05, 06, 09, 10), and the three replacements keep that balance. Every source URL loaded and is official and current. WAI-ARIA 1.2 is the W3C Recommendation of 06 June 2023 ("Authors MUST NOT use abstract roles in content."). WAI-ARIA 1.3 is the W3C Working Draft of 04 June 2026. ARIA in HTML is the W3C Recommendation of 11 August 2026; its button row does not allow heading, and section 3.1 warns against overriding interactive elements with non-interactive roles. MDN aria-valuenow lists only meter, scrollbar, separator, slider, spinbutton and progressbar, not global. MDN presentation role: "<h2 role=\"presentation\">... The heading role semantics are removed, but the content itself is still available." MDN aria-hidden: "doesn't visually hide anything" and "aria-hidden=\"false\" will not re-expose the element ... if any of its parents specify aria-hidden=\"true\"". Understanding 4.1.2 (Level A) covers \"components generated by scripts\". Cards that pass, with the source sentence that settles each:
- 01: Understanding 2.1.1 Note 1, "if using handwriting to enter text, the input technique (handwriting) requires path-dependent input but the underlying function (text input) does not".
- 02: the 2.1.2 SC text, "the user is advised of the method for moving focus away".
- 03: the 2.1.4 exception, "Active only on focus".
- 07: APG Keyboard Interface, "the tab and shift + tab keys move focus from one UI component to another while other keys, primarily the arrow keys, move focus inside of components". Minor issue: appliesTo is "WAI-ARIA 1.2" but the APG is not versioned; an empty string would be cleaner.

- 09: G1, "links that are visible only when they have focus can meet this success criterion". G1 is a Technique page, which is allowed only loosely by the source list. The Understanding 2.4.1 page would be the cleaner source, but G1 is the page that states the fact.
- 10: MDN describes how positive values behave and recommends "only use 0 and -1". The WHATWG HTML spec (not on the deck's allowed source list) settles validity: "must have a value that is a valid integer. Positive numbers specify the relative position".
- 12: MDN :focus-visible, "the UA ... determines via heuristics" and "when a text box needing user input has focus, focus is indicated".

- sr6-10 and sr6-11 (menu Escape key and menubar for navigation) and sr7-07 (Tab versus arrow keys).

verdicts.notes:
I checked all 12 r8 cards (all in web-accessibility-b2.json). Every source URL returned 200 and points to current official pages: 4 on MDN and 3 on the APG (dialog-modal, listbox, keyboard-interface). The section is balanced at 6 true (01, 03, 05, 06, 08, 09) and 6 false (02, 04, 07, 10, 11, 12). The one fix I suggest keeps that balance.

Evidence for the cards that pass:
- **01:** MDN tabindex says an element with any valid tabindex "can be focused with JavaScript (by calling the focus() method)" and that -1 is "not reachable via sequential keyboard navigation".
- **02:** The APG keyboard-interface page says "the user agent will scroll the newly focused element into view". It is also correct for focus(), whose preventScroll option defaults to false, and the statement says "by default".
  - Minor: this card leans on a DOM API default that javascript-fundamentals owns. It is kept because the APG names it as the benefit of roving tabindex.
- **04:** In the APG listbox recommended multi-select model, "Space: changes the selection state of the focused option" and Down Arrow "Moves focus to the next option". The page also says "DOM focus (the active element) is functionally distinct from the selected state."
- **05:** MDN showModal says "Elements inside the same document as the dialog, except the dialog and its descendants, become inert". It also supports the iframe caveat in the explanation.
- **06:** MDN dialog says "By default, a dialog invoked by the showModal() method can be dismissed by pressing the Esc key... When using <dialog>, this behavior is provided by the browser." The closedby attribute can change this, but the statement says "By default" and the prompt excludes closedby.
- **07:** MDN dialog says "focus is set on the first nested focusable element. Explicitly indicating the initial focus placement by using the autofocus attribute...". The HTML spec's focus delegate algorithm confirms it: it returns the autofocus delegate before the first focusable descendant (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/interaction.html).
- **08:** The APG dialog-modal page says "it may be advisable to set focus on the least destructive action, especially if undoing the action is difficult or impossible." The card's "suggests" matches that hedge.
- **09:** The APG says "focus returns to the element that invoked the dialog unless either: The invoking element no longer exists... The work flow design includes the following conditions that can occasionally make focusing a different element a more logical choice". The card keeps the qualifier the prompt asks for.
- **10:** MDN aria-modal says it "does not actually make the element modal. The features that make the element actually modal must be implemented by the developer." The APG note about application code preventing interaction agrees.
- **11:** MDN dialog says "The tabindex attribute must not be used on the <dialog> element" and "Do not add the tabindex property to the <dialog> element as it is not interactive and does not receive focus."
- **12:** MDN inert says inert content is "removed from the tab order and accessibility tree" and "hidden from assistive technologies as they are excluded from the accessibility tree". The HTML spec says "user agents do not expose the inert nodes to accessibility APIs or assistive technologies."

No r8 card rests on the same fact as an r6 or r7 card; r7's tabindex cards cover 0 and positive values, not -1 with focus().

Minor, not flagged: the APG-based cards (04, 08, 09) carry appliesTo "WAI-ARIA 1.2". The APG is not versioned with ARIA 1.2, so an empty string would be more accurate.

Cards that passed, with the evidence that settles each:
- 02: ARIA in HTML maps "img with empty alt and no accessible name" to role=none or role=presentation.
- 03: HTML-AAM 4.1.10 says to use the title attribute only "if the accessible name is still empty and there is no alt attribute". The card is correctly marked may_change because HTML-AAM is a Working Draft.
- 04: the functional images tutorial uses alt="Print this page" and says the alternative "should convey the action that will be initiated... rather than a description of the image". The explanation's "Print" is close enough.
- 05: the complex images tutorial says "a two-part text alternative is required".
- 06: Understanding 1.1.1 lists the failure "conveying information exclusively using CSS background images".
- 10: the CAPTCHA exception requires both text identifying the purpose and alternative CAPTCHA forms for different senses.
- 11: the text of 1.2.2 requires captions for prerecorded audio in synchronized media, with the clearly labeled media-alternative exception.

Of the 5 flags, 4 are weak_card: 01 is a truism, 08 is a near-copy of the technique's title, 09 is a near-copy of the SC's exception text, and 12 gives its answer away through the criterion's name. The fifth, 07, is a source_problem: MDN says "description" where AccName 1.2 says the SVG title is a name source. Every suggested fix keeps the original answer, so the section stays 6 true and 6 false.

I found no duplicates with other sections. The only cards elsewhere in the deck that touch these topics (sr3-10 caption, sr4-04 placeholder, sr11-08 resize text) rest on different facts. The scope item "missing alt attribute and how it is exposed" has no card in r10. That is not a defect, but it is open coverage if a card is replaced.

I checked all 12 r11 cards in content/raw/web-accessibility-b3.json (6 true, 6 false). None is flagged. All 9 source URLs returned HTTP 200 on 2026-10-04: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/ (W3C Recommendation 12 December 2024, the anchor #dfn-large-scale exists) and the WCAG22 Understanding pages contrast-minimum, contrast-enhanced, non-text-contrast, use-of-color, resize-text, reflow, text-spacing and content-on-hover-or-focus. Each card was checked against the normative text of WCAG 2.2.

What settles each card:
- 01 (true): 1.4.3 "has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, except for the following: Large Text ... at least 3:1".
- 02 (false): large scale is defined as "at least 18 point or 14 point bold or font size that would yield equivalent size for ... (CJK) fonts", so bold alone is not enough.
- 03 (true): the Understanding page says "the computed values should not be rounded (e.g., 4.499:1 would not meet the 4.5:1 threshold)".
- 04 (true): "Text that is part of a logo or brand name has no contrast requirement". The explanation's caveat is also on the Understanding page: "If logos normally have sufficient contrast but are presented with an insufficient contrast as an author choice ... not exempt".
- 05 (false): 1.4.6 asks for 7:1, but "Large-scale text ... at least 4.5:1".
- 06 (true): 1.4.11 covers "Visual information required to identify user interface components and states, except for inactive components or where the appearance ... is determined by the user agent and not modified by the author". The Understanding page adds "non-text indicators such as the check in a checkbox ... must have sufficient contrast to the adjacent colors".
- 07 (false): 1.4.1 says "Color is not used as the only visual means". The Understanding note counts only a lightness difference of at least 3:1 as an additional cue, so hue alone stays false.
- 08 (true): text "can be resized without assistive technology up to 200 percent". The Understanding page says the user agent's mechanisms include "zoom (of the entire page's content)".
- 09 (false): Reflow uses "a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels" ("equivalent to a starting viewport width of 1280 CSS pixels wide at 400% zoom").
- 10 (false): Note 1 says "Content is not required to use these text spacing values. The requirement is to ensure that when a user overrides the authored text spacing, content or functionality is not lost."
- 11 (true): the Hoverable condition reads "the pointer can be moved over the additional content without the additional content disappearing", and the user agent exception covers title tooltips.
- 12 (false): the Incidental exception exempts text "part of an inactive user interface component".

Rules check: no card is over 120 characters (longest 111) and no explanation is over 240 (longest 179). Average length is 99.7 for true statements and 98.3 for false ones. No card is only about a level. No threshold is made false by changing a number: card 09 changes the unit from CSS pixels to physical pixels, which is a real distinction. Every success criterion name and level is exact for WCAG 2.2. I found no duplicate or overlap with other sections; the only nearby cards are sr2-03 (Focus Appearance), sr2-05 and sr6-02, and they test different facts.

Two things below the flag threshold:
1. Several true statements carry exception qualifiers ("outside its exceptions" in 01, "active ... when authors style that mark" in 06, "authors'" in 11), while the false statements are blunt. A player could learn that a hedged statement is true. If the deck gets a polish pass, add a qualifier to one false card or remove one from a true card.
2. Card 07 (Use of Color, hue alone) is easy and close to a strawman, though it is defensible at difficulty 1. Its explanation could also mention that a lightness difference of 3:1 counts as an extra cue, as the Understanding note says.

flagged.urlStatus: 200, official W3C Understanding WCAG 2.2 page; supports the card
flagged.evidence: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/pause-stop-hide.html: "For any moving, blinking or scrolling information that (1) starts automatically, (2) lasts more than five seconds, and (3) is presented in parallel with other content, there is a mechanism for the user to pause, stop, or hide it unless the movement, blinking, or scrolling is part of an activity where it is essential"
flagged.problem: The answer is correct, but it is a name giveaway. The statement asks whether a pause control satisfies a criterion literally named "Pause, Stop, Hide", so a player who knows nothing can answer True from the name alone. The real conditions (starts automatically, lasts more than five seconds, runs in parallel with other content) are only in the explanation and are never tested.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replacement (answer true): "Pause, Stop, Hide (Level A) leaves out auto-starting motion that ends by itself within five seconds." Explanation: "Its moving, blinking and scrolling part covers content that starts automatically, lasts more than five seconds and runs in parallel with other content. Shorter motion needs no pause, stop or hide control." Same URL.

flagged.urlStatus: 200, official MDN page (Baseline widely available since January 2020); supports the card, and its example swaps a scale animation for an opacity "dissolve"
flagged.evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/At-rules/@media/prefers-reduced-motion: "the user prefers an interface that removes, reduces, or replaces motion-based animations"; also "The reduce keyword value evaluates as true; therefore, @media (prefers-reduced-motion) is equivalent to @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)."
flagged.problem: "Authors may replace ..." can hardly be false: no normative text forbids authors from any styling choice, so the hedge "may" makes it a near-truism that players answer True by guessing. It also adds to the section's hedge imbalance: both "may" statements in r12 (01 and 12) are true and none is false, which the RULES forbid.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replacement (answer true): "`@media (prefers-reduced-motion)` with no value matches the same users as `(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)`." Explanation: "The reduce keyword evaluates as true in a boolean context and no-preference as false, so the bare media query targets only users who asked for reduced motion." Same MDN URL, appliesTo "".

verdicts.notes:
I checked all 12 r12 cards (from web-accessibility-b3.json). The section is balanced at 6 true (01, 02, 05, 07, 09, 12) and 6 false (03, 04, 06, 08, 10, 11). Every source URL loads and is official.

Checks on the facts:
- WAI-ARIA 1.2 (https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/, Recommendation, 6 June 2023) says word for word: "Elements with the role alert have an implicit aria-live value of assertive", "role timer ... off", "role status ... polite". Its aria-relevant table lists "additions text (default)". So cards 02, 03, 04 and 06 are right.
- MDN Live regions supports card 01 ("changes to the element's content are only supposed to be announced when focus is on, or inside, the element") and card 07 ("Establish the live region before updating its content ... The most reliable way ... is to include them in the initial markup").
- MDN aria-atomic supports card 05 (true means "present the entire changed region as a whole").
- The 4.1.3 Understanding page supports card 08 ("can be presented to the user by assistive technologies without receiving focus", Level AA).
- The 2.3.1 Understanding page supports card 10. Flashing "cannot be allowed even for a second or it could cause a seizure", while blinking "can be allowed for a short time as long as it stops (or can be stopped)". That is exactly the 2.2.2 versus 2.3.1 confusion the card targets.
- The 2.3.3 Understanding page confirms Level AAA for card 11.

I found no duplicates elsewhere in the deck. No other section tests live regions, status messages or motion.

Borderline cards I did not flag:
- 02, 03 and 04 are three cards on implicit aria-live values. The scope allows this, and 03 and 04 share one false template. That is within the two-per-deck limit, but the template cannot be used for any other false card.
- 05 may be partly guessable from the word "atomic".
- 08 is easy because the success criterion's own text says "without receiving focus". It is still a realistic developer misconception.

Deck-wide hedge-verb count: card 01 keeps "may" as the prompt requires for announcement behaviour. With 12 replaced, r12 still has one true "may" (01) and no false one. A false card using a hedge verb would help the balance.

duplicates.why: Both test the alert versus status split in implicit aria-live (alert assertive, status polite). These are the two sides of one distinction, which RULES treat as one fact: anyone who knows that alert, not status, is the assertive role answers both, and sr12-03's explanation ('advisory updates rather than urgent interruptions') points straight at alert. Keep sr12-03, which encodes the realistic misconception. sr12-02 is plain recall and stacks 'By default' with 'implicit'.

conflictGroups.name: target-size-levels
conflictGroups.why: sr2-05 and sr2-06 print 'Target Size (Minimum) (Level AA)' and the 24 by 24 minimum, so sr2-11's claim that the 44 by 44 Target Size (Enhanced) is Level AA is easy to reject.

conflictGroups.name: enhanced-means-aaa
conflictGroups.why: sr2-10 and sr11-05 print '(Enhanced) (Level AAA)', and sr2-03 prints a sibling focus criterion at Level AAA. Seen next to them, sr2-02 and sr2-11 ('Enhanced ... Level AA') are given away.

conflictGroups.name: focus-not-obscured
conflictGroups.why: sr2-01 states that the Minimum criterion is Level AA and allows partial overlap, which strongly hints that the Enhanced criterion is the stricter Level AAA one (sr2-02).

conflictGroups.name: aria-adds-no-behaviour
conflictGroups.why: Same principle: an ARIA attribute declares semantics and the browser adds no behaviour. sr8-10's explanation ('describes modality ... it does not implement it') and sr5-04 ('authors keep ARIA state values synchronized') answer sr6-01 and sr9-06.

conflictGroups.name: modal-background-blocking
conflictGroups.why: A near mirror: native showModal() makes the background inert (true), while aria-modal on a custom dialog does not enforce blocking (false). sr8-10's explanation ('A custom dialog's code must prevent interaction') sets up the contrast with sr8-05.

conflictGroups.name: button-name-from-content
conflictGroups.why: sr4-05's statement presupposes 'the name supplied by the button's content', which is exactly the fact sr4-01 asks about.

conflictGroups.name: visible-label-required
conflictGroups.why: sr4-08 (APG prefers visible text) and sr4-04's explanation (placeholder is a fallback, not guaranteed output) hint that neither aria-label alone (sr9-02) nor a placeholder (sr9-08) can stand in for a visible label. sr9-02 and sr9-08 also share one false template.

conflictGroups.name: select-context-change
conflictGroups.why: A mirrored pair on the same scenario: a select that changes context on focus (On Focus, false) versus a select that changes context on change after advance warning (On Input, true).

conflictGroups.name: focus-order-document-order
conflictGroups.why: sr7-08 says browsers order tabindex=0 elements by document order, which gives away that CSS flex order does not change the tab sequence (sr7-11). sr7-04's explanation adds that visual and focus order may differ.

conflictGroups.name: identify-input-purpose-scope
conflictGroups.why: sr9-09's 'for eligible HTML fields' and the 'personal information the user enters' in its explanation reveal the user-data scope that makes sr9-10 false.

conflictGroups.name: media-text-alternatives
conflictGroups.why: A mirrored pair: 'a text alternative replaces the media requirement' is false for captions (sr10-11) and true for audio description or media alternative (sr10-12). sr10-11's explanation also mentions the media-alternative exception.

conflictGroups.name: image-purpose-not-appearance
conflictGroups.why: sr10-01's explanation ('a literal description of its appearance may miss why the image is on the page') gives away that 'Printer icon' is the wrong alternative for a Print button (sr10-04).

conflictGroups.name: short-alt-insufficient
conflictGroups.why: Same false template, 'a short identifying label is a complete or sufficient alternative' (chart alt, CAPTCHA purpose label). Seeing one answers the other.

conflictGroups.name: contrast-thresholds
conflictGroups.why: sr11-05's explanation gives 7:1 and 4.5:1 for large text, and sr11-02's explanation gives the large-scale definition. Together they hint at the 4.5:1 body-text floor in sr11-01 and at each other's answers.

conflictGroups.name: contrast-minimum-exceptions
conflictGroups.why: sr11-01 ('outside its exceptions') and sr11-04 (logotype exemption) prime the player that 1.4.3 has exemptions, which hints at the Incidental exemption that makes sr11-12 false. sr11-12's explanation names the Incidental exception.

conflictGroups.name: live-region-implicit-values
conflictGroups.why: Three cards on one table of implicit aria-live values. Alert being assertive answers status, and sr12-03 and sr12-04 share a word-for-word template. Never deal them together.

conflictGroups.name: stop-control-motion-vs-flash
conflictGroups.why: A near mirror: a pause or stop control satisfies Pause, Stop, Hide (true), but a Stop button does not exempt flashing content (false). Together they invite a compare-and-flip guess.

conflictGroups.name: spec-draft-status
conflictGroups.why: Mirrored status template: WCAG 3.0 claimed as a Recommendation (false) next to ARIA 1.3 'as a Working Draft' (true). sr1-12 (AGWG recommends WCAG 2.2 as the target) also implies that WCAG 3.0 is not the standard.

conflictGroups.name: conformance-scope
conflictGroups.why: sr1-05's explanation says every page of a process must conform and that an accessible step does not cover a nonconforming one, which hints that a page cannot exclude an inaccessible sidebar (sr1-04).

scan.tells:
I read all 144 cards (48 per batch, 6 true and 6 false in every section). Statement lengths are balanced: every section's true and false averages are within 5 characters (largest gaps: r6 99.2 true vs 95.0 false, r4 91.7 vs 95.5). The tells are in wording and templates.

1. Level as a predicate. Most criterion cards print the level in parentheses ('X (Level AA) ...'). The cards that state the level as the claim itself are all false: sr2-02, sr2-11, sr2-12 ('as a Level A requirement') and sr12-11, 4 of 4. No true level card exists, so 'criterion name without parentheses + Level' alone means False.

2. The word 'Enhanced'. Every statement containing it is false: sr2-02, sr2-10, sr2-11, sr11-05 (4 of 4). '(Minimum)' is 6 true / 3 false.

3. 'WAI-ARIA 1.2' named in the statement: 1 true / 6 false. True: sr12-02. False: sr4-06, sr5-03, sr5-05, sr9-12, sr12-03, sr12-04. 'WAI-ARIA 1.2 lets/permits/treats ...' is 4 of 4 false (sr4-06, sr5-03, sr5-05, sr9-12).

4. A success criterion as the subject with a permissive verb (permits, accepts, lets): 11 true / 2 false. True: sr2-01, sr2-09, sr3-08, sr4-12, sr7-03, sr7-09, sr9-05, sr10-09, sr10-12, sr11-08, sr12-09. False: sr2-04, sr7-06. 'permits' anywhere is 7 true / 3 false, so hedge verbs mark true statements, against RULES.

5. Other skewed words.
   - 'Browsers' as the subject: 3 true / 7 false. True: sr3-01, sr5-08, sr7-08. False: sr3-02, sr3-07, sr6-01, sr7-11, sr7-12, sr8-07, sr8-12. Mostly b2, where it is 2 true / 5 false.
   - 'treats': 0 true / 3 false (sr5-05, sr10-05, sr10-10).
   - 'includes': 1 true / 3 false (true sr2-05; false sr2-10, sr9-10, sr12-06).
   - 'exempt(s)': 1 true / 3 false (true sr11-04; false sr7-01, sr10-06, sr12-10).
   - 'calls for': 3 true / 0 false (sr4-09, sr7-02, sr9-03).
   - A 'when ...' condition clause: 13 true / 7 false.

6. False-statement templates used more than twice (RULES allows two).
   a. 'An ARIA attribute makes the browser provide behaviour': sr6-01, sr8-10, sr9-06.
   b. 'A criterion or document mandates one specific method': sr1-08, sr3-11, sr4-10, sr9-04, sr12-08.
   c. 'X exempts content from criterion Y': sr7-01, sr10-06, sr12-10.
   d. 'An AAA criterion is Level AA': sr2-02, sr2-11, sr12-11.
   e. 'A partial cue is sufficient': sr9-02, sr9-06, sr11-02 and sr11-07 (all with 'alone'), plus sr10-05 ('sufficient') and sr10-10 ('complete solution'). That is 6 false cards.

7. Templates that mark the answer.
   - sr12-03 and sr12-04 use the same sentence, 'In WAI-ARIA 1.2, the `X` role gives its updates the implicit aria-live="Y" priority', and both are false. The true sibling sr12-02 is worded differently ('By default, WAI-ARIA 1.2 gives the alert role ...').
   - 'The WAI tutorial ...' is false 2 of 2 (sr10-04, sr10-05); 'The WAI technique ...' is true (sr10-08).
   - 'ARIA in HTML recommends/permits' is false 2 of 2 (sr5-02, sr5-06); 'ARIA in HTML maps' is true (sr10-02).

8. Where b3 (GPT-6.1 Sol) differs from b1 and b2.
   - It inserts a lowercase 'authors' actor mid-sentence ('when authors ...', 'lets authors', 'requires authors'') in 10 statements, against 3 in b1 and 2 in b2. In b3, 9 of those 10 are true (sr9-01, sr9-03, sr9-05, sr9-11, sr11-03, sr11-06, sr11-08, sr11-11, sr12-07); only sr12-08 is false.
   - 'alone' is false 4 of 4 in b3 (sr9-02, sr9-06, sr11-02, sr11-07), but true 2 of 2 in b2 (sr5-08, sr6-02). The two models use the word in opposite directions.
   - In b3, every 'criterion + permits/lets/accepts' statement is true (sr9-05, sr10-09, sr10-12, sr11-08, sr12-09).
   - 7 of 48 b3 statements start with 'Authors', against 2 in b1 and 4 in b2.
   - b3 explanations are longer: 164 characters on average, against 141 in b1 and 150 in b2. They use 'calls for' 4 times (0 in b1 and b2) and repeat the '(Level X)' tag in the explanation 26 times, against 15 in b1 and 7 in b2.
   - b2's true explanations run about 10 characters longer than its false ones (155 vs 146).

9. sr4-01 ('<button>Save</button> is named "Save"') is close to a truism, and sr4-05's statement presupposes its answer.

rewrite.reason: source_problem: the cited intro page does not say guidelines are untestable. The Layers of Guidance section of the Recommendation says it ('The guidelines are not testable, but provide the framework and overall objectives'). Statement, answer and explanation are unchanged.
rewrite.statement: WCAG guidelines provide the pass-or-fail checks used to decide conformance.
rewrite.explanation: Success criteria provide the testable requirements. Guidelines state the broader goals rather than individual pass-or-fail checks.
rewrite.misconception: The guidelines themselves are the testable conformance requirements.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2: WCAG 2 Layers of Guidance

rewrite.reason: weak_card (near-copy of the backwards-compatibility slogan), rewritten because dropping sr1-01, sr1-10 and sr1-12 would leave r1 at 3 true out of 9. The replacement is in scope (WCAG 2.2 does not deprecate or supersede 2.1 and 2.0) and was confirmed on TR/WCAG22: 'The publication of WCAG 2.2 does not deprecate or supersede WCAG 2.0 or WCAG 2.1. While WCAG 2.0 and WCAG 2.1 remain W3C Recommendations, the W3C advises the use of WCAG 2.2'. factKey: wcag22-does-not-supersede-21-20.
rewrite.statement: Publishing WCAG 2.2 left WCAG 2.1 and 2.0 in place as current W3C Recommendations.
rewrite.explanation: WCAG 2.2 does not deprecate or supersede WCAG 2.0 or 2.1, which remain W3C Recommendations, though W3C advises using WCAG 2.2 to maximize future applicability.

rewrite.reason: ambiguous: 'authors still assess 4.1.1' describes practice, and WCAG 2.2 itself says authors bound to 2.0/2.1 'may need to continue to test and report 4.1.1'. Rewritten as a true statement of what WCAG 2.2 contains, plus the reason the Understanding page gives ('Assistive technology used to do their own parsing of markup, but now rely on the browser'). Turning it true moves r2 from 4/6 to 5/5 after the two drops, and removes one of the always-false 'level as predicate' cards. Removal is tested once in the deck.
rewrite.statement: In WCAG 2.2, 4.1.1 Parsing is obsolete and removed because assistive technology now relies on browsers to parse HTML.
rewrite.explanation: Assistive technology used to parse markup itself. Many issues that once failed Parsing now fail Info and Relationships or Name, Role, Value instead.

rewrite.reason: weak_card (strawman: bold CSS creating th semantics), rewritten because dropping all four flagged r3 cards would leave 8. The verifier's replacement was confirmed on MDN main: 'A document mustn't have more than one <main> element that doesn't have the hidden attribute specified.' It adds coverage of the main landmark. factKey: single-visible-main-element.
rewrite.statement: HTML allows two visible `<main>` elements on one page when each has a unique accessible label.
rewrite.explanation: A document may have only one main element without the hidden attribute, so a label cannot make a second visible main valid.
rewrite.misconception: A unique accessible label lets a page repeat the main landmark the way it can repeat nav or region landmarks.
rewrite.sourceTitle: <main>: The Main element - MDN Web Docs

rewrite.reason: source_problem: MDN aria-label never states replace-versus-append. The APG says: 'If aria-label is applied to an element with one of the roles that supports naming from child content, content contained in the element and its descendants is hidden from assistive technology users.' Statement and answer kept; explanation takes the verifier's sourced wording.
rewrite.statement: On a button, `aria-label` appends its text to the name supplied by the button's content.
rewrite.explanation: If aria-label is set on a button, its value replaces the name the button would get from its content; the content is hidden from assistive technology users rather than appended.
rewrite.misconception: aria-label supplements rather than replaces the button's content-derived name.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Providing Accessible Names and Descriptions: Naming with a String Attribute Via aria-label - ARIA Authoring Practices Guide

rewrite.reason: tell: statements that name 'WAI-ARIA 1.2' are 0 true / 6 false after sr12-02 is dropped, and 'WAI-ARIA 1.2 lets/permits/treats' is 4 of 4 false. This removes the prefix and the hedge verb 'permits'. Fact (generic prohibits naming) and answer (false) are unchanged.
rewrite.statement: `aria-label` on a plain `<div>` with its implicit generic role gives that div a valid accessible name.
rewrite.explanation: The generic role prohibits accessible naming. Adding aria-label to a plain div is not a valid way to name it under that role.
rewrite.misconception: aria-label is valid as a naming mechanism on elements with any implicit role.
rewrite.sourceTitle: ARIA: generic role - MDN Web Docs

rewrite.reason: tell: removes the 'WAI-ARIA 1.2 treats' prefix (always false). Fact (aria-valuenow is role-specific, not global) and answer (false) are kept. The source moved to the WAI-ARIA 1.2 Global States and Properties list, which lists aria-label and aria-describedby but not aria-valuenow, so the whole card can be checked there.
rewrite.statement: `aria-valuenow` is a global ARIA property, like `aria-label` and `aria-describedby`.
rewrite.explanation: aria-valuenow is role-specific: WAI-ARIA 1.2 uses it on range roles such as slider, spinbutton and scrollbar, while aria-label and aria-describedby are global.
rewrite.misconception: ARIA value properties are global attributes that work independently of the element's role.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Accessible Rich Internet Applications (WAI-ARIA) 1.2: Global States and Properties

edits.notes:
I opened every page a rewrite or source fix relies on on 2026-10-04. Pages and quotes:
- TR/WCAG22 (non-deprecation sentence, #wcag-2-layers-of-guidance, 4.1.1 'Obsolete and removed').
- Understanding parsing ('now rely on the browser').
- MDN main (only one main without hidden).
- APG names-and-descriptions (#naming_with_a_string_attribute_via_aria-label).
- APG menubar-navigation example (Caution and Disclosure Pattern).
- MDN aria-pressed ('more than one item controlled by the button').
- MDN Ordering flex items and MDN reading-flow (Experimental, Limited availability, default normal follows DOM order).
- G13 and Understanding on-input.
- WAI decorative images tutorial (Example 3).
- Understanding images-of-text.
- AccName 1.2 (Working Draft, 2 October 2026; #comp_host_language_label names SVG title).
- MDN prefers-reduced-motion (bare query equals reduce).
- Understanding focus-not-obscured-minimum (partial obscuring allowed; sticky-footer examples).
- MDN aria-atomic.
- WAI-ARIA 1.2 (anchors #global_states and #timer exist; aria-valuenow is not global; timer is off).

Decisions:
- Weak cards were dropped wherever the section stayed at 9 or more cards with at least 4 of 10 on each side. Rewrites were used only where needed: r1 (sr1-10), r3 (sr3-09), r10 (sr10-01, sr10-09) and r12 (sr12-12).
- I did not take sr3-12's suggested replacement: the Understanding 'should' for single-page-app titles is advisory, so 'calls for' would be ambiguous.
- sr2-12 was rewritten as a true card, not the suggested false 'WCAG 2.2 keeps 4.1.1 at Level A'. That evens r2 at 5/5 and removes one always-false level-as-predicate card.
- I did not use the verifier's sr7-11 explanation about reading-flow, because the cited Ordering page never mentions reading-flow. 'By default' in the statement covers the exception.
- sr10-09 departs slightly from the suggestion. 'with matching alt text' was added so the criterion name does not give the answer.

Tell rewrites (5): sr2-01, sr4-06, sr5-05, sr12-04, sr12-05. They target the strongest patterns:
- The 'WAI-ARIA 1.2' prefix is now 2 true / 3 false; it was 0/6 after sr12-02 dropped.
- 'Criterion + permits' for true statements.
- The sr12-03/sr12-04 shared template.

Residual tells I could not fix without changing facts:
- 'Enhanced' and level-as-predicate are still always false (sr2-02, sr2-10, sr2-11, sr11-05, sr12-11). They are covered by the enhanced-means-aaa conflict group.
- 'Criterion + lets/accepts' remains mostly true: sr2-09, sr3-08, sr4-12, sr7-03, sr7-09, sr9-05, sr11-08. sr4-12 was left alone because the Label in Name Understanding page lists interspersed words as a possible failure, so rewording it is risky.

Conflict groups:
- Removed, because only one member was left: button-name-from-content, select-context-change, media-text-alternatives, stop-control-motion-vs-flash.
- Removed: image-purpose-not-appearance, because the sr10-01 rewrite no longer gives away sr10-04.
- Added empty-alt-decorative (sr10-01 and sr10-02): sr10-02 shows alt="" as decorative markup.
- Added aria-label-global-vs-generic (sr4-06 and sr5-05): sr5-05 names aria-label as a global property.

Metadata to update with the rewrites:

- sr12-12 appliesTo "" and factKey prefers-reduced-motion-bare-query-equals-reduce.
- sr3-09 factKey single-visible-main-element.

I took the wording lens fix because 'W3C advises using WCAG 2.2' in the old explanation gives away sr1-12 (AGWG recommends WCAG 2.2 as the conformance target). It names the version, does not say WCAG 2.1 removed the criterion and keeps the point about Info and Relationships / Name, Role, Value, so it respects the 4.1.1 trap rule. The Understanding page says 'Assistive technology used to do their own parsing of markup, but now rely on the browser.' Statement 117 characters, and it is the only card in the deck that tests the removal.

cards.explanation: A document may have only one main element without the hidden attribute, so a label cannot make a second visible main valid.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep the card. I fetched MDN <main> myself: 'A document mustn't have more than one <main> element that doesn't have the hidden attribute specified.' factKey: single-visible-main-element.

cards.statement: On a button, `aria-label` appends its text to the name supplied by the button's content.
cards.explanation: If aria-label is set on a button, its value replaces the name the button would get from its content; the content is hidden from assistive technology users rather than appended.
cards.reason: The text stays as the editor wrote it; the fix is the source URL anchor, as the fact lens says. That section says aria-label 'hides descendant content from assistive technology users and replaces it with the value of aria-label' (confirmed).

cards.statement: `aria-label` on a plain `<div>` with its implicit generic role gives that div a valid accessible name.
cards.explanation: The generic role prohibits accessible naming. Adding aria-label to a plain div is not a valid way to name it under that role.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep the card. Generic is 'Name From: prohibited' in WAI-ARIA 1.2, and MDN says aria-label is prohibited on generic. It follows the prompt's accessible-name trap rule. The tell-carrying prefix and hedge verb are gone. appliesTo stays WAI-ARIA 1.2.

cards.statement: `aria-valuenow` is a global ARIA property, like `aria-label` and `aria-describedby`.
cards.explanation: aria-valuenow is role-specific: WAI-ARIA 1.2 uses it on range roles such as slider, spinbutton and scrollbar, while aria-label and aria-describedby are global.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep the card. The WAI-ARIA 1.2 Global States and Properties list contains aria-label and aria-describedby but not aria-valuenow. aria-valuenow is used in meter, range, scrollbar, separator, slider and spinbutton, so 'such as' is accurate.

cards.statement: In WAI-ARIA 1.2, `aria-pressed="mixed"` marks a toggle button whose controlled items hold differing values.
cards.explanation: aria-pressed is tri-state: true, false or mixed. Mixed means the items the button controls do not all share the same value; the default, undefined, means the element is not a toggle.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep the card. WAI-ARIA 1.2 and MDN both say 'A value of mixed means that the values of more than one item controlled by the button do not all share the same value', and WAI-ARIA 1.2 says the button is not a toggle button when the attribute is absent. Using the WAI-ARIA 1.2 prefix on a true card balances that tell.
